title: Chapter 7 — The Chapel
paragraphs: In this same New Bedford stands a Whaleman's Chapel, and few moody fishermen, shortly bound for the Indian Ocean or Pacific, fail to pay it a Sunday visit. I certainly didn't.

Returning from my first morning stroll, I set out again on this particular errand. The sky had changed from clear, sunny cold to driving sleet and mist. Wrapping myself in my shaggy jacket of the cloth called bearskin, I fought my way through the stubborn storm. Inside, I found a small, scattered congregation of sailors and sailors' wives and widows. A muffled silence reigned, broken only at times by the shrieks of the storm. Each worshipper seemed deliberately sitting apart from the others, as if each grief were an island, incommunicable. The chaplain hadn't arrived yet. These silent islands of men and women sat steadfastly gazing at several marble tablets with black borders, set into the walls on either side of the pulpit. Three of them read something like this, though I don't pretend to quote exactly:

SACRED TO THE MEMORY OF JOHN TALBOT, Who, at the age of eighteen, was lost overboard, Near the Isle of Desolation, off Patagonia, November 1st, 1836. THIS TABLET Is erected to his Memory BY HIS SISTER.

SACRED TO THE MEMORY OF ROBERT LONG, WILLIS ELLERY, NATHAN COLEMAN, WALTER CANNY, SETH MACY, AND SAMUEL GLEIG, Forming one of the boats' crews OF THE SHIP ELIZA Who were towed out of sight by a Whale, On the Off-shore Ground in the PACIFIC, December 31st, 1839. THIS MARBLE Is here placed by their surviving SHIPMATES.

SACRED TO THE MEMORY OF The late CAPTAIN EZEKIEL HARDY, Who in the bows of his boat was killed by a Sperm Whale on the coast of Japan, August 3d, 1833. THIS TABLET Is erected to his Memory BY HIS WIDOW.

Shaking the sleet from my ice-glazed hat and jacket, I took a seat near the door, and on turning sideways I was surprised to find Queequeg close by. The solemnity of the scene had affected him, and his face wore a wondering look of disbelieving curiosity. This savage was the only one there who seemed to notice me come in, because he was the only one who couldn't read, and so wasn't reading those cold inscriptions on the wall. Whether any relatives of the seamen named there were in the congregation now, I couldn't tell; but the fishery has so many unrecorded accidents, and several of the women present so plainly wore the look, if not the mourning dress, of some unending grief, that I feel certain the people gathered in front of me were those in whose unhealing hearts the sight of those bleak tablets, in sympathy, made the old wounds bleed again.

Oh! You whose dead lie buried beneath the green grass, who can stand among flowers and say — here, right here, lies my beloved — you do not know the desolation that broods in hearts like these. What bitter blanks in those black-bordered marbles that cover no ashes! What despair in those immovable inscriptions! What deadly voids and unbidden infidelities in lines that seem to gnaw at all Faith, and refuse resurrection to beings who have perished nowhere, without a grave. Those tablets might as well stand in the cave of Elephanta as here.

In what census of living creatures are the dead of mankind included? Why does a universal proverb say of them that they tell no tales, though they hold more secrets than the Goodwin Sands? How is it that to the name of someone who departed yesterday for the other world we prefix so significant and unbelieving a word, and yet give him no such title if he merely embarks for the remotest Indies of this living earth? Why do the Life Insurance Companies pay out death-forfeitures on immortals? In what eternal, unstirring paralysis and deadly, hopeless trance does ancient Adam still lie, who died sixty full centuries ago? How is it that we still refuse to be comforted for those whom we nevertheless maintain are dwelling in unspeakable bliss? Why do all the living strive so hard to hush all the dead? Why does the mere rumor of a knocking in a tomb terrify a whole city? None of these things is without its meaning.
But Faith, like a jackal, feeds among the tombs, and even from these dead doubts she gathers her most vital hope.

I hardly need to tell with what feelings, on the eve of a Nantucket voyage, I looked at those marble tablets, and by the murky light of that darkened, doleful day read the fate of the whalemen who had gone before me. Yes, Ishmael, the same fate may be yours. But somehow I grew merry again. Delightful inducements to embark, a fine chance for promotion, it seems — yes, a stove-in boat will make me an immortal by brevet, an honorary rank. Yes, there is death in this business of whaling — a speechlessly quick, chaotic bundling of a man into Eternity. But what then? I think we have hugely mistaken this matter of Life and Death. I think that what they call my shadow here on earth is my true substance. I think that in looking at spiritual things, we are too much like oysters observing the sun through the water, and thinking that thick water the thinnest of air. I think my body is only the dregs of my better being. In fact, take my body whoever will — take it, I say — it is not me. And therefore three cheers for Nantucket; and let a stove boat and a stove body come when they will, for stave in my soul Jove himself cannot.
